62. The writ petitioner also filed Affidavit-in-Reply dated 18.05.2010 denying the statements and allegations made in affidavit-in-opposition and stated that the writ petitioner was never aware of any Government committee nor any of its report. Prior to issuance of the impugned Memo, the petitioner never heard about any committee as stated in the affidavit-in-opposition. The respondents issued the impugned memo in gross violation of the principles of natural justice. The right of the petitioner is protected under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 and the Non-Agriculture Tenancy Act, 1949. The provisions of these Acts have not been excluded in the registered lease deed. Since the full salami of the lease including the land rent have been paid, the petitioner has acquired vested right, which cannot be taken away without giving an opportunity of being heard before passing an order affecting the right of a person. 

 108. Mr. Rafique-ul-Haque the learned Senior Advocate appearing in all the above writ petitions for the petitioners has taken us through the writ petition and Annexure to the writ petition and referred to Annexure —B to the writ petition No. 639 of 2010 the lease deed and drawn our attention to the deed, wherein it has been stated "'all* Itx erx ghkf mat ?ft kftFsir and submits that the land is Non Agricultural Land and is guided by Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and the respondents should follow the procedure as laid down in section- 7, 8, 70 and 71 which runs thus:- 

 (1) if any non-agricultural land has been held with or without any lease having been entered into by the landlord and the tenant from before the commencement of the Transfer of Property Act. 1882 , (IV of 1882) or if the origin of any tenancy is unknown, or 

 (2) if the non-agricultural land comprised in any tenancy which has been or is created after the commencement of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, (IV of 1882), has been held for a period of not less than twelve years without any lease in writing, or 

 (1) Notwithstanding any thing contained in any other law for the time being in force or in any contract, where any non-agricultural land is held under a lease in writing for a term of not less than twelve years specified in such lease, the tenant holding such land shall on the ex-piration of the period so specified he entitled to the renewal of such lease for perpetuity on such fair and reasonable rent as may be 1 (determined under chapter XIV of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. (E.B. Act No. XXVIII of 1951). 

 (3) "A tenant holding non-agricultural land comprised in a tenancy to which the provisions of sub-section (1) apply shall not be ejected by his landlord from such land during the term specified in the lease, nor at any time after the tenant has exercised his right of renewal, except on the ground that he has used such land in a manner which renders it unfit for use for any of the purposes specified in section 

 " 70. No ejectment except in execution of decree. — No Non-agricultural tenant shall be ejected from the tenancy or from any non-agricultural land which he holds except in execution of a decree of a competent Civil Court. 

 106. Duration of certain leases in absence of written contract or local usage — In the absence of a contract or local law or usage to the contrary, a lease of immovable property for agricultural or manufacturing purposes shall be deemed to be a lease from year to year, terminable, on the part of either lessor or lessee, by six months' notice expiring with the end of a year of the tenancy; and a lease of immovable property for any other purpose shall be deemed to be a lease from month to month, terminable, on the part of either lessor or lessee, by fifteen days' notice expiring with the end of a month of the tenancy. 

 149. Mr. Islam then submits that the parliamentary standing committee has got no authority whatsoever to inquiry into the matter and the 58result of inquiry also is not binding upon the petitioner's as the tenancy has been created under Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and as such the provision of Transfer of Property Act is applicable. The alleged inquiry to have made by the parliamentary standing Committee or any recommendation made by the said committee has got no legal implication in the matter as the same has not been referred by the parliament and no consent of the speaker was taken as contemplated under Rule 100 and 110 of procedure of parliament and as such the same is liable to be declared to have been passed without lawful authority. 

 172. Mr. Majumder has also submitted that the respondents cannot issue the impugned order cancelling the long term lease as the same is guided by Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. 1949 and Transfer of Property Act and as such the impugned order is liable to be declared to have issued without lawful authority. He submits further that the respondents also have not followed the Principle of Natural Justice for which a show cause notice is a must before cancellation of the long term lease and in this score also the impugned order is liable to be declared to have issued without lawful authority. 

 181. Mr. Majumder has also submitted that the respondents cannot issue the impugned order cancelling the long term lease as the same is guided by Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. 1949 and Transfer of Property Act and as such the impugned order is liable to be declared to have issued without lawful authority. He submits further that the respondents also have not followed the Principle of Natural Justice for which a show cause notice is a must before cancellation of the long term lease and in this score also the impugned order is liable to be declared to have issued without lawful authority. 

 225. Mr. Ahmed has given emphasis contending that the respondents have not followed the due process of law in as much as an agreement signed and concluded on receipt of consideration money the Government cannot resort to take away the right accrued to the petitioner in as much as the petitioner should be given an opportunity of being heard as contemplated under the principle of natural justice and as such a show cause notice is a must before cancellation of the lease. The government also failed the comply the provision of Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, Transfer of Property Act of 1882 and section 39 of the Specific Relief Act and thereby the notice of cancellation of the long term lease is an abuse of the power which is not contemplated under any law of the land and as such the impugned notice is liable to be declared to have issued without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 

 261. Mr. Rokan Uddin Mahmud, the learned Senior Advocate appearing for the petitioner in both the above writ petitions has taken us through the writ petitions and Annexure to the writ petitions and made submissions touching the points from all corner and submitted that admitted by the government has granted long term lease of Non-Agricultural Land guided under Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act 1949 and the same Act has been made applicable of the provisions of Transfer of Property Act 1882. The instrument is Registered under the Registration Act 1898 and if such instrument requires to be cancelled, in that case step has to be taken under section 39 of the Specific Relief Act but the respondents have not followed the aforesaid provisions of law but with certain imaginary contention has cancelled the lease which is illegal and as such, the impugned order is liable to be declared to have issued without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 

 302. Mr. Kamal-ul Alam, the learned Senior Advocate appearing for the petitioner has taken us through the writ petition and Annexure to the writ petition and very candidly adopted the submissions and the decisions referred by Mr. Rafique-ul-Haque senior Advocate to support his contention. Apart from the adoption of the submissions of Mr. Haque, Mr. Kamal-ul Alam has taken us to section 81 A and 81 B and submitted that the lease deed has been executed in favour of the lessee by the competent authority and the lease has been duly registered under the provision of clause (d) of sub-section (1) of section 17 of the Registration Act of 1908 and the Provision of section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act is applicable and as such, the respondents had to determine the tenancy by notice. He contends further the respondents also have not followed the principle of natural justice in as much as before cancellation of the lease deed a show cause notice should have been served but in this case also the respondents have not served any notice and as such the respondents have violated the principle of natural justice. 

 "40. Learned Judges of the High Court appear to have made some confusion in interpreting the said definition clause and in holding the appellant to be a non-agricultural tenant within the meaning of that clause on the view that he was a holder of a lease in perpetuity. The appellant is obviously not a holder of a lease in perpetuity, as the preamble of the Indenture of the lease clearly provides that it is a lease for the specified- period of 99 years. Term no 23(3) (a) of the Indenture does no doubt reserve the right of option for the lessee for the renewal of the lease after the expiry of the specified period of 99 years and in case of exercise of such option the lessor shall have to renew the lease but on such terms, covenants and conditions and for such period as the lessor may determine. There is no doubt that this is not a lease in perpetuity but is one for a fixed period, though a lease in perpetuity is unlike in England. provided in section 105 of the Transfer of property Act. Although there seems to have been some misapprehension in the said observation of the learned Judges of the High Court in respect of the meaning of non-agricultural tenant, their conclusion that the appellant is a non-agricultural tenant cannot be taken exception to in view: of the fact that he having held lands for purposes other than agriculture or horticulture comes under the first part of the said definition clause and being the owner of the buildings standing on such land does not come under the second part of the said clause. According to the said definition, a person who is a tenant in respect of the land as well as the building standing thereon on the basis of lease which is not perpetual is not a non-agricultural tenant within the meaning of the said definition clause and he may be tenant coming within the purview of the premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963. According to the definition clause quoted above, only such a person will be a non-agricultural tenant as has constructed the building, if any, in his own right on the land leased out to him by the owner of such land. It is, therefore, abundantly clear that the appellant is a tenant as well as a non-agricultural tenant within the meaning of sub-section (2) of section 81A of The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and his rights and liabilities are, according to the said provision, to be governed by the terms of the Indenture of his lease and the provisions of the Transfer of Property Act except in regard to his powers of sub-letting and in matters relating to determination, enhancement and reduction of rent, which shall be regulated according to the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, notwithstanding anything contrary thereto in the terms of the lease or elsewhere. there is, therefore no difficulty in holding that the learned judges of the High Court were correct in taking the view that the appellant is assesses under the provisions of the two taxing Statutes as have been referred to above."
